content: The crude rate of medically treated falls per person per year was 0.061 in the intervention group and 0.072 in the control group, corresponding to a relative risk (RR) of 0.86 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.66–1.12). This indicates a reduction in the rate of falls requiring medical treatment in the intervention group compared to the control group. Additionally, after adjusting for factors such as age, history of previous falls, sex, and ethnic origin, the intervention group demonstrated a 26% reduction in the rate of fall-related injuries occurring at home per year compared to the control group (RR: 0.74, 95% CI: 0.58–0.94). The study was methodologically robust, with proper randomization (using an electronic coin toss) and allocation procedures. While participants were not blinded to their group assignment, the coders assessing outcomes were masked to allocation status. The intervention group received an additional educational pamphlet, but the specific impact of the educational material could not be separated from the effects of home modifications. A systematic review on home injuries conducted for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines included several studies. For example, Kendrick et al. (2015) conducted a multicenter case-control study in the United Kingdom to identify risk and protective factors for falls from furniture in children aged 0–4 years. Cases included children who experienced a fall from furniture and sought medical attention, while controls were children of the same age and sex who did not experience such falls. Controls were matched on age, sex, calendar time, and general practice. Recruitment involved contacting potential participants during medical attendance or within 72 hours via telephone or mail. The study aimed to recruit an average of four controls per case, and additional controls were sourced from other ongoing studies when necessary. Another study by Kamei et al. (2015) in Tokyo, Japan, evaluated the effectiveness of a home hazard modification program in reducing falls among community-dwelling older adults aged 65 years and above. The intervention included education and practical training on home safety using a model mock-up of a typical Japanese home. Stewart et al. (2016) conducted a multicenter case-control study in the United Kingdom to identify modifiable risk factors for scald injuries in children under five years of age. Cases included children with scald injuries occurring at home who sought medical attention, while controls were children without scald injuries matched on age and sex. Recruitment involved contacting participants during medical attendance or via postal invitations. The study was of good quality overall, but participation rates in the case and control groups were unclear. A systematic review also assessed the impact of various interventions on home injuries. For example, Campbell et al. (2005) conducted a randomized controlled trial in New Zealand to evaluate the effectiveness of home safety modifications in reducing falls among visually impaired adults aged 75 years and older. The study demonstrated a reduction in serious injurious falls, with moderate-quality evidence supporting the findings. Other studies included in the review examined the impact of interventions such as smoke alarms, safety gates, and window guards on injury prevention. For instance, Pressley et al. (2005) found that window guard legislation significantly reduced fall-related injuries in children. Similarly, Chamania et al. (2015) reported that replacing kerosene lamps with solar/LED lamps in rural India eliminated unintentional burns in participating households. Overall, the systematic review highlighted the importance of home safety interventions in reducing injuries, but it also identified limitations such as low participation rates, inconsistent results, and potential biases in some studies.
